title: How do people explain where the world comes from?
essentialQuestion: What questions do origin accounts answer, and how can we learn about them with respect?
learningGoal: Explain why different accounts of beginnings answer different kinds of questions, and describe how to learn about them with respect.

warmUp.question: Which question about how things began would you most like to ask?
options: How did the stars and the Earth form?
Why is there a world at all?
Who first told a story, and why?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Could one kind of evidence answer all three questions? Why or why not?

cards.title: A founding story from Tallgrass Valley

sources.caption: A story that elders in the town of Tallgrass Valley tell
details: Long ago, the valley was dry and empty.
Two families followed a river into the valley to find water.
They planted a fig tree together and promised to share its fruit.
Today, people in the valley still plant a tree when a child is born.

cards.title: Three questions about beginnings
items: Question A: How did the stars and the Earth form?
Question B: What does the Tallgrass story teach people about sharing?
Question C: Who first told the Tallgrass story, and when was it written down?

sections.heading: People everywhere tell accounts of beginnings
sections.text: People all over the world have asked where the world came from. Many communities have an origin account. It tells how something began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe that God created the heavens and the earth. Many Hindus see time as a great cycle. In this cycle, the universe is made, ends and then begins again. Many Aboriginal peoples of Australia tell of ancestral beings who shaped the land, the water and the animals. Groups in Africa, the Americas and the Pacific also pass on their own accounts in stories and songs. Even a small town can have an origin account, like the founding story of Tallgrass Valley. Accounts like these carry a group's beliefs and values.
sections.simpler: People all over the world ask how it all began. Many groups have an origin account. It tells how things began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe God made the world. Many Hindus believe the world ends and starts again. This happens again and again. In Australia, many Aboriginal people tell of beings from long ago. These beings made the land and the animals. Groups in Africa and the Pacific have their own accounts. Our made-up town, Tallgrass Valley, has one too. These accounts hold beliefs and values.

sections.heading: Different accounts answer different questions
sections.text: Each kind of account can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things happen in nature. They use evidence that people can see, measure and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and has been growing ever since. Faith accounts and cultural accounts often answer other questions. Why is there a world? What matters most? How should people treat each other? Historians ask a third kind of question: who told an account, when, and why. Look again at the three questions about beginnings. Each one needs a different kind of answer.
sections.simpler: Each account can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things happen in nature. They use evidence they can see and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. Faith accounts often ask other things. Why is there a world? How should we live? Historians ask who told an account, and why. Each question needs its own kind of answer.

sections.heading: We learn about accounts with respect
sections.text: In this lesson, we learn about accounts, but we do not judge them or rank them. Respect means describing each account carefully and never mocking it. We say "Many people believe ..." for a faith account and "Scientists explain ..." for a science account. Many people hold both a faith account and a science account, and many scientists are also people of faith. Nobody has to share what they believe. If you are not sure how to describe an account, check a trusted source or ask a teacher.
sections.simpler: Here, we learn about accounts. We do not judge them. We do not say one is best. Respect means we describe each account with care. We never laugh at it. Say "Many people believe" for faith. Say "Scientists explain" for science. Many people accept both kinds of account. You do not have to share your own beliefs.

glossary.definition: A story or explanation of how something began.
glossary.example: The Tallgrass story about two families and a fig tree is an origin account.

glossary.definition: Something a person holds to be true, often about faith or life.
glossary.example: People in many communities share their beliefs through stories and songs.

glossary.definition: An idea about what is important or right.
glossary.example: Sharing is a value in the Tallgrass story.

glossary.definition: Information that helps show whether something is true.
glossary.example: Scientists measure light from faraway stars and use it as evidence.

glossary.definition: Treating people and their ideas with care.
glossary.example: We show respect when we describe every account carefully.

write.prompt: Choose two of the three questions about beginnings. Explain why each one needs a different kind of answer.
sentenceStarters: To answer it, people could use ...
These questions need different answers because ...
selfCheck: I chose two of the three questions.
I said what kind of answer each question needs.
I wrote about each account with respect.
write.example: The first question asks how the stars and the Earth formed. To answer it, people could use evidence that scientists measure. For example, they study light from faraway stars. The second question asks what the Tallgrass story teaches about sharing. To answer it, people could listen to the elders. They could think about the promise to share the fig tree. These questions need different answers. One asks how something happened in nature. The other asks what matters to a group of people.

speak.partnerTask: Take turns reading one of the three questions about beginnings. Your partner says what kind of question it is and who could help answer it.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud: "A science account answers questions like ... A faith or cultural account answers questions like ..."

watch.title: The Big Bang Explained
watch.why: It shows one science account of the start of the universe, so you can see what kind of question science answers and what evidence it uses.
watch.beforeQuestion: What kind of evidence do you think scientists use to study the early universe?
watch.afterQuestion: What is one thing scientists explain in the video, and what evidence do they use?
watch.summary: This video gives a science account of how the universe began. Scientists explain that it began about 13.8 billion years ago. At first, it was very small and very hot. Since then, it has grown bigger and cooler. Scientists use evidence they can measure. For example, they see that faraway groups of stars are moving away from us. This shows that the universe is still growing. They also find a faint glow left over from when the universe was very young. A science account like this answers questions about how things happen in nature. Questions about meaning, or about how to live, need other kinds of answers. Many people value both a science account and a faith account.
keyPoints: Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago.
Science uses evidence that people can measure and test.
Different accounts answer different kinds of questions.
watch.contentNote: This video gives a science account only. Introduce it as one kind of account that answers 'how' questions about nature; it does not judge or replace faith accounts. Please preview it with a local educator before use.

replacementSuggestion.title: Origin Stories | OER Project
replacementSuggestion.why: It looks at origin stories from many cultures, not only the science account, so it fits the lesson's question better than a Big Bang explainer. Watch it in full first: OER Project's origin-story materials place faith accounts beside a science 'Big History' story and retell some traditions, so a local educator should check how it presents them.

visual.description: Three simple boxes side by side, each with one question and a plain icon. A telescope: 'How did it happen?' (science: evidence we can measure). A small tree: 'Why? What matters most?' (faith and cultural accounts: meaning and values). A scroll: 'Who told it, when and why?' (history). One line under all three boxes reads 'Different questions need different kinds of answers.' Do not use religious symbols or pictures of holy figures.
visual.alt: Three boxes show three kinds of questions about beginnings: how it happened, why it matters, and who told the account.

educatorNotes: Please ask a local educator, ideally from the learners' own communities, to review this lesson before it is used. Most pilot learners are likely to come from Muslim-majority communities, and others hold different beliefs or none.
Never ask learners to state, defend or rank their own beliefs. If a learner shares a belief, thank them and move on; do not debate it.
The lesson describes faith accounts only in general terms and does not retell any scripture. If you add an example, keep it general and check the wording with someone from that tradition.
The current video gives only a science account. A replacement about origin stories from many cultures is suggested, but please watch it in full before switching.
changes: Cut the reading from about 300 words at grade 9 to three short sections at the target level; 'simpler English' is now much shorter and easier.
Replaced the claim types (empirical, historical, value, corroboration) with one simpler idea: different accounts answer different kinds of questions (how, why and what matters, who told it).
Added a fictional, non-religious founding story (Tallgrass Valley) so learners practise on neutral material.
Added short, general descriptions of accounts from several traditions and regions, using 'Many people believe' and 'Scientists explain'; no scripture is retold and no account is ranked.
Said clearly that people can hold both a faith account and a science account, and that nobody has to share their beliefs.
Lightly reworded the essential question for reading level ('examine them respectfully' became 'learn about them with respect'); the meaning is the same.
Added a content note and educator notes asking for local review, and suggested a replacement video about origin stories from many cultures.
